messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dorothy is a 73-year-old married woman of European descent who works as a QA engineer, a role that demands precision and predictability. She came to therapy at her husband’s gentle insistence, though she admits she has felt “stuck” for decades. Her childhood trauma began when she was six years old, living with her mother and stepfather. Her stepfather, a man her mother trusted implicitly, would punish her for minor infractions—spilling milk, speaking out of turn—by locking her in a dark closet for hours. The worst incident occurred when she was eight: after she accidentally broke a vase, he dragged her by the arm, threw her into the closet, and held the door shut while she screamed and pounded on the wood. She remembers the sound of his breathing on the other side, the smell of dust and mothballs, and the certainty that no one would come. What haunts her most is the betrayal—she had trusted him, and her mother had done nothing.

Decades later, Dorothy’s life is still shaped by that closet. She describes her memory of the event as photographic, as if she can flip through still images in her mind: the crack of light under the door, the pattern on the wallpaper, the feel of her own tears on her cheeks. Yet sometimes, when she tries to tell someone what happened, the words vanish. She knows what occurred but cannot find language to describe it, and in those moments she feels completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger. This emotional distance is a relief, but it also fuels a deeper shame: she believes she will never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened, for being too small and too scared to fight back.

These negative appraisals are reinforced whenever she encounters a trigger. Uncertainty is the most pervasive: a change in schedule at work, an unexpected email from a male colleague, even a cloudy forecast can send her into a spiral. Funerals and cemeteries are unbearable because the grief of others reminds her of the helplessness she felt as a child. But the most potent trigger is male presence. Being alone with a man—any man, even her own son-in-law—makes her body react before her mind has time to think. Her heart races, her palms sweat, and she becomes hypervigilant, scanning for sudden movements. “I’m on guard before I even know why,” she says. She has come to believe that she cannot stop bad things from happening to her, that the world is fundamentally unsafe, and that her only protection is constant watchfulness.

Dorothy’s avoidance has shaped her life. At work, she schedules meetings only in open-plan areas and never stays late if a male colleague is in the office. She has stopped attending family gatherings where men might be present, and she has not visited her mother’s grave in years. Her husband, a kind and patient man, has learned to announce his movements before entering a room, but even that does not fully calm her. The causal loop is tightening: each trigger brings a surge of threat, which strengthens her belief that she is helpless, which makes the memory of the closet feel more vivid and inescapable. And because she cannot find words for it, the memory feels even more isolating, which deepens her guilt and shame.

What finally brought Dorothy to therapy was a moment of crisis at work. A new male manager asked her to join him in his office to discuss a project. She felt her body go cold, her throat close, and she excused herself to the bathroom, where she stayed for twenty minutes, trembling. She realized then that she could no longer function. She is afraid that therapy will force her to speak about what she has never been able to put into words, but she is also desperate to stop the cycle. What she hopes for most is to feel safe in her own body, to walk through the world without the constant sense that danger is waiting just behind a closed door.
